segments.spokenText: Part 4. From textile waste to usable fibre. You now have one minute to read questions 31 to 40.

A discarded garment may look like a straightforward source of material, but recovering useful fibre requires a sequence of decisions. Today we'll follow a simplified mechanical recycling process for a stream of donated textiles. This is not a description of every industrial method. Different fabrics and desired outputs require different treatments. The point is to understand why collecting a large mass of clothing does not automatically create an equal mass of high-quality new cloth. Each stage changes what is available to the next, and some losses are unavoidable.

segments.spokenText: The first decision is whether an item should enter recycling at all. Wearable garments may be more useful through reuse. Sorting workers therefore separate items that can still be worn from those intended for material recovery. This stage requires judgement about condition and practical demand, not just age. A nearly new garment with severe damage may be unsuitable for reuse, while an older coat can remain serviceable. Reuse and recycling serve related purposes, but mixing their outputs in one impressive total can hide what actually happens to the collected clothing.

segments.spokenText: Next, workers examine composition. Labels provide a starting point, though they may be missing or unreliable. A blend contains more than one fibre type, and that combination can make recovery harder. A process designed for a relatively uniform stream may perform poorly on mixed materials. Some facilities use instruments to help identify composition, but readings still need to be interpreted within the process's limits. Sorting is not merely putting red garments in one pile and blue garments in another; colour and composition answer different production questions.

segments.spokenText: Colour separation can nevertheless be useful. Keeping similar colours together may reduce the need for later dyeing when the recovered fibre is used in a suitable product. This does not mean every faded shirt can become a new shirt of exactly the same appearance. The final use depends on fibre quality and the specifications of the next manufacturer. A less demanding product may be the realistic destination for some material. Calling that outcome a failure without considering the available alternatives can obscure a useful recovery, while calling it identical to garment-to-garment recycling can also mislead.

segments.spokenText: Before cutting, workers remove hard components such as buttons and metal fasteners. These can damage machinery or remain as unwanted fragments in the output. Removal takes time, and garment construction affects how easy it is. A designer choosing decorative hardware may therefore influence a future recycling cost without seeing it at the design stage. After preparation, the textile is cut into smaller pieces. The pieces pass through equipment that pulls the fabric apart, releasing fibres rather than preserving the original woven or knitted structure.

segments.spokenText: Mechanical opening usually shortens fibres. Length matters because very short fibres can be difficult to spin into a strong new yarn. The recovered material may be blended with a proportion of new fibre to meet the intended requirement. The proportion is not a universal recipe: it varies with the input and product. A claim about recycled content should state what is being measured and in which component. A small recycled lining does not make the whole garment entirely recycled, even if the marketing photograph draws attention to the lining.

segments.spokenText: The output undergoes checks before a manufacturer uses it. Tests may include strength and the presence of unwanted contamination. Sampling needs to represent a batch, not only its cleanest corner. Failed material may enter another suitable route rather than the same spinning process, but that route should be recorded. Mass balances help account for useful output, removed components and losses. Without such records, a collection programme can report what entered the facility while leaving the destination of much of it unexplained.

segments.spokenText: The broader lesson is that recycling begins before a garment is discarded. Material choice, construction and accurate labelling affect later options. Collection remains necessary, but the quality of the route after collection determines what the activity achieves. A transparent account follows the material through the process, states the intended product and acknowledges limitations. It offers more useful guidance than an unqualified claim that all donated clothing returns to the wardrobe in an endless loop.
